summary: get_user_role() (legacy-token path) had no AuthDB fallback - a demoted/removed principal's still-valid API token resolved at pre-revocation role indefinitely.
Denied-login branch never evicted the stale users_ cache entry on AuthDB reporting a user inactive.

Unauthenticated NUL-truncated username matched the real row at the PG text-format boundary while the mangled string became a distinct, never-evicted cache key; security-guardian re-review additionally found an account-lockout bypass vector (unbounded PBKDF2 guessing).
Mangled-username session bypassed remove_user()/update_role()'s session-invalidation match, defeating CHAOS-T1-001.
ABA race: role-value compare-guard fooled by promote-then-demote-to-same-value inside PBKDF2 window - CH-1.

CH-3: unauthenticated login spray exhausting the PG pool could transiently demote every legacy-token admin request fleet-wide via .value_or(Role::user). Re-derived down: production PG pool defaults to 16 (not 4, the unit-test fixture's shrunk value), and the existing 10/s/IP rate limiter + lockout_status()'s own pre-existing unconditional PG read (default lockout_threshold=5) mean this isn't a NEW zero-cost amplification the way CH-3's original framing assumed.

find_user_or_hydrate's try_emplace can land after a concurrent remove_user()'s erase(), resurrecting a stale cache entry. Scoped Gate 7 re-check traced every consumer path (self-recheck, cross-caller recheck, get_user_role(), list_users()) and confirmed the resurrection can never survive past the call that created it and no consumer ever trusts the cache as authoritative - E6-capped (wrong outcome proven unable to occur), not blocking.

reactivate_user()'s wholesale cache replace reset role_version to 0, reopening a narrower ABA window; falsified the 'only via u64 wraparound' doc claim. Found independently by 4 of 5 fix-round-1 reviewers.
First CH-1 regression test exercised demote-to-different-role, which old and new guards handle identically - not the round-trip-to-same-value ABA case the finding is actually about.

get_user_role() now makes an unconditional per-request PG round-trip on every legacy-token request; a store degradation floors to Role::user. Deliberate accepted tradeoff, disclosed in-code, generation-gated-cache follow-up unfiled until now.
Changelog fragment omits the PG-availability-coupling disclosure and doesn't name the new metric.
3 deferred items referenced in code comments with no linked issue: std::expected refactor, alert rule, generation-gated cache.

get_user_role()'s nullopt conflates not-found vs. store-error; pre-existing callers audit reason=user_not_found on a transient PG hiccup - factually wrong audit entry. Independently found twice, explicitly self-deferred by commit message to Gate 8, never actually tracked until now.
verify_password()'s own users_.erase eviction branch (from 4392c725d) untested - authenticate()'s equivalent path is covered.

erase() previously fired on ANY get_user() error, not just UserNotFound, contradicting a 'now-stale' comment. VERIFIED FIXED by direct code read this session: current recheck_role_after_credential_check discriminates UserNotFound (evicts) from any other error (fails closed, does not touch cache).
Race-hook test only drives authenticate(), never verify_password() (same guarded code, different call site).

set_role_recheck_race_hook_for_test is unguarded and injects behavior (not just state) into the auth hot path - more powerful than the existing _for_test convention. Zero production callers confirmed.
find_user_or_hydrate()'s DbError branch has no metric of its own; only a genuine blind spot when auth_lockout_threshold=0 (lockout disabled).
string_to_role() silently parses any non-admin value to Role::user, no logging.
Hardcoded PG-pool-size-4 duplicated 3x across test fixtures, no shared constant.
Stale docstring contradicts an adjacent, already-corrected NOTE comment in the same test case.

record_failed_login's independent write during a hydrate-read failure could misaudit a store hiccup as a bad credential - hand-off to compliance-officer/consistency-auditor, not yet independently picked up.
No genuine two-thread TSan test for the race-hook mechanism; both new tests are deterministic single-thread.
No REST-level cold-cache/DbError test through POST /login.

get_user()'s bare try_acquire_for() (no retry) is denied immediately, fleet-wide, for the pool's existing 200ms-5s connect-backoff breaker window (documented at auth_db.cpp:170-177, issue #2396's acquire_with_retry exists for exactly this and is unused here). During that window every legacy-token admin request floors to Role::user (ApiTokenStore's own token_cache_ survives the blip since it's decoupled from role resolution, so only the role check fails) and auth_routes.cpp's legacy-fallback audit_log writes a misleading 'non-admin role denied' row for a principal who is actually admin - a truth/audit-integrity gap during exactly the SOC2-relevant window, reachable via an ordinary transient PG blip with no attacker required (pure E0, more mundane than the CH-3 spray framing).
classification: correctness/audit-integrity, second-opinion (Fable) finding on the CH-3 scoping decision

summary: New row-lock-blocking test spawned a std::thread and could hit a throwing REQUIRE before joining it, unwinding past a still-joinable thread and calling std::terminate() on failure - would abort the whole test shard instead of failing one test.
writer_was_still_blocked was computed as !writer_finished.load() with no check that the writer thread had actually started - trivially true if the writer never ran at all.

The blocking test's discriminating window (writer-thread-entry + 20ms hold) was thin enough that an unblocked update_role() doing two DB round trips could plausibly still be mid-flight at 20ms on a loaded runner, passing even if the row lock were broken - a latent false-green risk.

An earlier draft documented a second, separate 'cross-replica case' residual alongside the check-then-mint gap. Wrong: Postgres row locks serialize at the database-engine level, not per-process, so a racing writer from a different replica sharing the same Postgres primary is serialized by the same row lock exactly like a same-process writer. Verified empirically against a live Postgres instance in both directions; independently re-confirmed by authdb via the pre-existing HA session-invalidation mechanism.

The safety-argument comment for recheck_role_locked leaned on the /login per-username stripe mutex (auth_routes.cpp's login_lock_for) as if it universally guarded the call; it doesn't, since the stripe is only taken when auth_lockout_threshold > 0, an operator-configurable setting that can be 0.

Commit fa2c0e209's title contains 'close #4107', a GitHub auto-close keyword, but the issue (re-scoped to the still-open check-then-mint gap) is not actually closed by this fix - merging would silently auto-close a genuinely open, HIGH-derived tracking issue.
disposition: escalated-to-operator (cannot amend an already-made commit per standing no-amend convention without explicit request; needs Dave's decision on PR body wording or a follow-up commit before merge)

summary: Six doc/comment sites (role_version field doc, role_version_epoch_ doc, two update_role() branch comments, reactivate_user() comment, authenticate() call-site comment) still described the retired case-2/case-3 version-counter mechanism after the row-locking rewrite superseded it; a dead test forwarder (recheck_role_after_credential_check_for_test) had zero remaining callers; one duplicate comment line existed on the new test-hook field.

with_txn_for(kWriteTimeout) only bounds the connection ACQUIRE; once inside the transaction, the FOR UPDATE row-lock WAIT is bounded by PgPool::connect_one's per-connection lock_timeout (10000ms default, pg_pool.hpp), roughly 5x kWriteTimeout - a contended lock under the /login stripe could block far longer than the safety-argument comment implied.

The row-lock-blocking test's writer-thread-entry + 200ms wall-clock margin (already hardened once from a 20ms margin) was empirically demonstrated flaky under genuine full-suite concurrent load: one failure in two full-suite runs (writer_call_duration=4.8ms, writer never reached the lock-contending statement within the hold window).

Doc claimed the row lock 'serializes against update_role()/reactivate_user()' without qualification. Only true in one direction: reactivate_user()'s UPDATE has no is_active filter, but recheck_role_locked's SELECT is is_active-filtered, so it never contends with a FRESH reactivate_user() call against an already-inactive row (excluded before any lock is taken) - an overclaim, though the safety conclusion itself was not wrong.

mfa_verify_login_code (the pre-existing MFA-replay-guard row lock this fix explicitly modeled itself on) has the identical with_txn_for(kWriteTimeout, SELECT...FOR UPDATE) shape with no SET LOCAL lock_timeout - same latent gap, not introduced or touched by this PR.

writer.join() ran unconditionally, but several recheck_role_locked early-return paths (lease-acquire timeout, the new SET LOCAL failure branch, a failed/empty SELECT) skip the test hook entirely, leaving writer non-joinable - join() on a non-joinable std::thread throws std::system_error, producing a confusing 'unexpected exception' instead of a clean assertion failure under exactly the pool-contention conditions this commit hardens against.

The new pg_stat_activity poll query (added to replace the flaky wall-clock proof) had no datname/pid scoping - pg_stat_activity is cluster-wide, and this repo runs a 4-way sharded [pg] test topology against one shared Postgres instance, so an unrelated shard's own lock contention on a same-named auth.users table could false-positive this observation even if THIS test's row lock were silently broken. Raised for floor adjudication (false-green test offered as closure evidence for a formerly-BLOCKING-derived finding) rather than pre-decided.

Nothing proved the new SET LOCAL lock_timeout statement actually fires in practice (only that it compiles and the happy path passes) - no test drove a genuine lock-contention scenario to confirm the recheck fails closed near kWriteTimeout rather than hanging toward the connection's 10s default.

The pg_stat_activity poll window (400 iterations x 5ms = 2000ms) exactly matched kWriteTimeout with zero theoretical margin - in the worst case the poll could exhaust before the writer even issued its UPDATE.

A 50ms sleep after observing the writer blocked added no additional proof - pg_stat_activity reflects live backend state synchronously, not an MVCC snapshot, so the positive observation was already a real-time fact.

The reworded reactivate_user() asymmetry doc (pass 9, 4107-M7) attributed the no-block outcome to 'no writer in flight,' which is not the actual Postgres discriminator - under READ COMMITTED, a row whose last-committed state already fails the is_active=TRUE qualifier is never a lock candidate regardless of whether a writer happens to be concurrently uncommitted at that instant. The safety conclusion was correct; the causal explanation could mislead a future maintainer.

Confirmed both prescribed fixes (writer.join() joinable() guard; pg_stat_activity datname/pid scoping) landed as directed. New 'holder' PgConn resource (second TEST_CASE) independently reviewed: RAII-correct, safe on all four REQUIRE unwind paths, destructed before auth_db teardown by declaration order, no leak/double-free/lifetime hazard.

A comment misattributed the pool's 10000ms lock_timeout default to the side 'holder' connection, which is opened directly via PQconnectdb and bypasses the pool's startup option entirely - inert to test correctness (holder never itself waits on a lock) but a Rule-3 comment-truth nit.

Confirmed the reworded reactivate_user() READ-COMMITTED-snapshot doc is technically correct; independently ran the new SET LOCAL lock_timeout test 6x directly against live Postgres (2011-2012ms each run, sub-ms variance - a server-side timer interrupt, not a client poll loop); confirmed padded poll window introduces no idle-in-transaction risk (verified no such GUC is configured in the pool) and re-ran the 30 surrounding [cold_cache] tests (326 assertions) green; confirmed the dead-sleep removal's reasoning is correct.

The lock_timeout test's upper bound (6000ms) was not tight on the evidence gathered (6x direct runs all ~2011ms, ~4000ms/200% headroom) but offered free extra headroom for a more jitter-prone runner (Wee Tam/Windows) without moving the fix-absent discriminator (~10011ms).
